items.summary: SONOLOGYST's 'Deep Sea' turns NOAA hydroacoustic ocean recordings into a dark ambient album, out 4 December 2026 on CD and digital via Cold Spring.
items.fullText:
Italian sound artist SONOLOGYST releases Deep Sea. Studies on Hydroacoustic Recordings from Oceanic Depths on 4 December 2026 through Cold Spring Records, on CD in a 6-panel digipak and digitally. SONOLOGYST is the solo project of Raffaele Pezzella, who also curates the Unexplained Sounds Group platform.

“Deep Sea” is built from hydroacoustic material drawn from underwater monitoring archives, including long-term hydrophone recordings collected by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for scientific observation of oceanic systems. Those recordings are treated as sound data and reworked through spectral analysis, transformation, morphing and synthesis. Low-frequency pressure waves, marine organism vocalisations, seismic activity and ambient underwater noise are folded into a continuous acoustic field shaped by depth, temperature gradients and water mass stratification, resulting in a dark ambient, drone and isolationist album. The cover shows a spectrogram of one of the source NOAA recordings.

The album runs across eight tracks: “Abyssal Gradient” (7:18), “Subsurface Thermocline Oscillation” (5:43), “Sonar Field” (4:15), “Pelagic Drift” (7:24), “Aphotic Life Forms” (2:45), “Hydrophone Array at 4,000 m” (6:32), “Mariana Trench” (10:37) and “Hydroacoustic Archive” (16:35).

“Deep Sea” follows a run of Cold Spring releases built around scientific and archival source material, including Sonologyst’s “Shortwave Spectrum”, which worked from recordings of clandestine number stations, and an earlier album built from NASA space probe signals. SONOLOGYST’s catalogue on Cold Spring also includes the album Interdimensional.

About SONOLOGYST

SONOLOGYST is the solo project of Italian sound artist Raffaele Pezzella. The project works from early electronic and electroacoustic experimentation of the 1950s and 1960s toward the present possibilities of electronic instruments, with a focus on the relationships between music and science and between music and other art forms, including literature and mythology. Pezzella describes the project’s output as moving between scientific sonic documentary and psychedelic abstraction.

Pezzella is also the curator of Unexplained Sounds Group, a multimedia platform documenting the underground experimental music scene worldwide, which has released numerous “Anthology of Experimental Music” compilations covering different countries and regions. SONOLOGYST has released albums on Cold Spring Records and Eighth Tower Records, including “Dust Of Human Race,” “Interdimensional” and “Shortwave Spectrum.” “Deep Sea. Studies on Hydroacoustic Recordings from Oceanic Depths” is out 4 December 2026 via Cold Spring.

items.title: Purr Machine return with ‘Animal Crossing’ video, first new music since 2007
items.summary: Purr Machine release 'Animal Crossing', first single since 2007's 'Starry', ahead of a new album due via 33.3 Music Collective in January 2027.
items.fullText:
American electro-industrial duo Purr Machine has released Animal Crossing, a single and video that is the band’s first new music since its 2007 album “Starry.” The song and video arrived on 15 November, and a full album of the same name follows on 15 January 2027 via 33.3 Music Collective.

Purr Machine is the project of vocalist Betsy Martin, previously of the Phoenix band Caterwaul, and bassist and programmer Kevin Kipnis, formerly of the deathrock group Kommunity FK. The pair formed Purr Machine in 1996 in North Hollywood, California, releasing the EP “Speak Clearly” in 1999 and the debut album “Ging Ging” in 2000, both via Re-Constriction. After a seven-year gap, they returned with “Starry” in 2007 on No Bliss Lost Records, featuring contributions from Chris Vrenna (Nine Inch Nails), William Faith (Faith and the Muse) and Statik (Collide). “Animal Crossing” ends a 19-year wait for new Purr Machine material.

The song takes its title and subject from the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing, a wildlife overpass near the duo’s home in Southern California. Kipnis filmed footage of the crossing’s construction, which the video pairs with wildlife imagery. Purr Machine described the song as being about “the instinct to keep moving through an uncertain world,” drawing a line between wildlife finding a way across and the risks and hope involved in finding one’s own way through life.

“Animal Crossing” is streaming on Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, Pandora, Tidal and iHeartRadio.

About Purr Machine

Vocalist Betsy Martin and bassist and programmer Kevin Kipnis formed Purr Machine in 1996 in North Hollywood, California, after previously recording together as the duo Kore. Martin had earlier been a member of the Phoenix-based band Caterwaul; Kipnis had played bass in the Los Angeles deathrock group Kommunity FK.

Purr Machine released its debut EP, “Speak Clearly,” in 1999 on Re-Constriction, followed by the debut album “Ging Ging” in 2000, also on Re-Constriction. Guitarist Kirk Hellie, of Pink Noise Test, joined the duo for that period. After a hiatus, Purr Machine returned in 2007 with the album “Starry” on No Bliss Lost Records, which featured contributions from Chris Vrenna of Nine Inch Nails, William Faith of Faith and the Muse, and Statik of Collide.

Now working again as a duo, Martin and Kipnis release “Animal Crossing” as a single and video on 15 November 2026, with the album of the same name due on 15 January 2027 via 33.3 Music Collective.

items.title: GUILT shares video for ‘Show Me Around’, first single from debut album
items.summary: GUILT's 'Show Me Around' is the first single from the Brussels duo's debut album 'Holding On // Letting Go', due 12 February 2027 via Afterstorm Records.
items.fullText:
Belgian electronic duo GUILT has released Show Me Around, the first single from its debut album “Holding On // Letting Go.” The album is due on 12 February 2027 on vinyl, CD and digital, self-released through the band’s own imprint, Afterstorm Records. GUILT is François Custers and Pierre Van Vlaenderen, the latter also a member of Endless Dive.

The accompanying video was directed by Custers. GUILT stated: “For the video, we wanted a very minimalist, confrontational setting. Throughout its opening, the video acts almost as a counterpoint to the song’s lyrics: where the words evoke multiple landscapes, the environment stays deliberately bare, underlining the inner dimension of the journey the song describes. The image then pulls us into a gradual descent, where jolting images follow one another like disjointed flashes, tracing the movement of an inner flight and the fading reminiscences of a dream.”

“Show Me Around” is streaming on Bandcamp and other digital platforms, but not on Spotify: GUILT left the platform more than a year ago. The band built a companion website, guiltshowmearound.netlify.app, that lets Spotify users still hear the track while redirecting them toward a direct donation to the band instead. GUILT stated: “We left Spotify more than a year ago now, for a whole series of ethical reasons. That was obviously a decision with heavy consequences for a developing project like ours, and we wanted to communicate about it in a slightly original way. That’s how we came up with the idea of building a website aimed directly at Spotify users, letting them still hear the song while also making them aware of why we left the platform. Conceived as a ‘Spotify offset,’ the site lets people offset Spotify’s negative impact by giving fairer compensation, through a donation of one euro or more. We first tried this on our previous release, and the donations received were three times higher than our best revenue ever recorded on Spotify.”

“Holding On // Letting Go” follows GUILT’s 2024 EP “State of Denialism,” released on 25 October that year. The album was written, recorded and arranged by Custers (vocals, synthesiser, production) and Van Vlaenderen (synthesiser, bass, production), and mixed and mastered by Adrien Schockert. Drums on “Show Me Around” and “My Awesome Flood” were played by Martin Grégoire; drums on “Hellomother” were played by Denis Baeten, recorded at 1935 Studio. Artwork is by Graphka design.

François Custers commented on the album: “Holding On // Letting Go is the result of several years spent maturing our collaboration as musicians who came from more of a rock background but ended up united around alternative electronic music. I think it’s above all an album that escapes boxes and labels, one where we wanted to venture in multiple directions while keeping a strongly recognisable identity that I hope is our own. It’s a particular album, not only for its stylistic identity but simply because it almost didn’t exist.”

About GUILT

GUILT is the Brussels-based duo of François Custers and Pierre Van Vlaenderen, the latter also known for the project Endless Dive. The band combines electronic production with dark, vocal-led songwriting, built around Custers’ lyrics and voice alongside synthesiser and bass work from both members.

GUILT released its debut EP, “State of Denialism,” on 25 October 2024, exploring denial as a response to contemporary crises. “Show Me Around” is the first single from the duo’s debut album, “Holding On // Letting Go,” written and recorded over roughly three years and due on 12 February 2027 via the band’s own Afterstorm Records, on vinyl, CD and digital.

items.title: Maciek Frett interview: ‘I give them the stage’
items.summary: Maciek Frett, founder of Wrocław Industrial Festival, discusses 25 editions, Sala Gotycka's DIY years, and industrial music's role today.
items.fullText:
Maciek Frett, founder, artistic director and curator of Wrocław Industrial Festival, discusses the event’s 25th edition in an interview with Karo Kratochwil. The anniversary edition ran in Wrocław from 5 to 8 November 2026, with first-wave industrial act SPK performing in its new incarnation as SPKtR and new collaborations staged for the occasion, including Flint Glass with Ah Cama-Sotz and Meta Meat with N.U. Unruh.

The conversation covers the festival’s DIY history at Sala Gotycka, the changing identity of industrial music since Throbbing Gristle, and how a 25-year-old event avoids becoming a prisoner of its own success.

Maciek Frett interview

Karo: I’ve been attending WIF since its second edition. I remember the freezing Sala Gotycka, Ania’s vegetarian bigos and that wonderful DIY chaos. Watching the anniversary film, did you recognise the festival you remember, or did you discover a different version of its history through other people’s eyes?

Maciek: Human memory works in such a way that everyone remembers events from the past in their own individual manner. Besides, the way we perceive those events changes with time. I remember very clearly both WIF’s difficult beginnings and all the subsequent stages we went through. Other people’s memories and stories are more of an invitation for me to reflect on the relativity of memory and the passage of time than an attempt to redefine what I remember myself.

To be precise, we organised the first WIF in 2001 at La Fete, a club located in a former Festung Breslau bunker. The programme consisted mainly of bands we were friends with from Poland, the Czech Republic and Germany. The festival turned out to be quite a success, attracting people from all over Poland.

After a year’s break caused by various personal circumstances, we returned in 2003 and have organised the festival every year since. We found a new home in Sala Gotycka, which was completely unused at the time. There were bare brick walls and beautiful Gothic vaults, which I’m sure you remember.

For the next twelve years, until the venue acquired a new tenant, the Stary Klasztor club, we prepared every edition by building practically the entire infrastructure from scratch. We carried the stage, sound equipment and bar furnishings upstairs on our own backs and arranged the dressing rooms ourselves. We even had to hoist a ladder through a window because there was no way to manoeuvre it around the narrow staircase.

Those were the days of total DIY. We did absolutely everything ourselves: putting up posters, preparing food for the bands, handling the entire logistics and then spending a week cleaning the venue after the festival. That also included the obligatory repainting of the staircase in white, because it served as the smoking area back then.

Those were formative years, and I feel enormous affection for them. We were so young.

On the other hand, I cannot imagine working under those conditions today. I’m 53 now, and after every festival I’m so mentally and physically drained that it takes me several weeks to return to normal. If we were still operating the way we did twenty-five years ago, I’d probably be a complete wreck by now.

Karo: Now that the anniversary edition is behind us, how would you personally assess it? What made you proudest, what surprised you, and was there anything you felt didn’t quite work as you’d hoped?

Maciek: Not even seven days have passed since the last sound faded from the stage. For me, the festival is still going on, and it will continue for several more weeks. Now comes the least exciting part of the work, which the audience generally never sees: reports, invoices and all that boring paperwork.

At this stage, very little has really sunk in. I’m simply exhausted, trying to finally get some sleep and return to a normal rhythm, but my control-freak nature keeps getting the better of me. For now, I mainly see what we could have done better and what needs improving for the next edition, rather than the things I should be proud of. I believe that moment will come.

On the other hand, the opinions, messages of thanks and comments we’re receiving through social media and email suggest that things really did go very well.

I’m particularly pleased with the interest in the festival. Every ticket was sold, and people travelled to Wrocław from all over the world, including places as distant as Hong Kong, Japan, Mexico and even Peru.

The concert programme and all the accompanying events went exactly as planned. But only the small group of people directly involved in organising everything really knows how much energy, stress and effort that required.

So a more objective assessment will have to wait, although I realise that complete objectivity is probably impossible when it comes to me and WIF. I think I’ll be able to look at everything more calmly in two or perhaps three months, once the dust has finally settled.

Karo: The XXV edition brought Graeme and Robert Revell’s SPKtR to Wrocław, alongside special collaborations such as Flint Glass with Ah Cama-Sotz and Meta Meat with N.U. Unruh. Which of these ideas was the greatest creative or organisational gamble, and did the performances match what you had imagined?

Maciek: First of all, I’m proud that these exceptional collaborations, as you rightly describe them, received their world stage premieres during the twenty-fifth edition of WIF.

The same applies to the return, after almost forty years, of an absolute legend of first-wave industrial music, SPK, in its new incarnation. The first concert of their European tour took place in Wrocław, and that was undoubtedly a major event.

Every unusual performance of this kind, and collaborative projects are probably the best example, involves a certain degree of risk. Something extraordinary might happen, but the whole thing could just as easily turn into an artistic disaster.

However, I wouldn’t like to comment on what I personally enjoyed more or less from a musical perspective. I’m the festival’s curator and producer; I remain rather in the shadows, behind the stage. My role is to create the best possible conditions for artists to present their creative potential to an audience.

In other words, I give them the stage. That’s where my role ends. What they do with that opportunity is entirely up to them.

Ultimately, the most important thing is the audience and its reaction. We see and feel that reaction after every song and every concert. The audience is the final judge.

Their excitement, emotion, applause or the degree to which they are moved provide the best, and perhaps even the most objective, assessment of what has happened on stage.

Judging by the audience’s reactions at this year’s WIF, I think things went very well, and at certain moments exceptionally well.

Karo: When WIF began in 2001, Poland was still outside the European Union. Today, most of your audience comes from abroad. How has that internationalisation changed the festival’s relationship with Wrocław itself? Is there a gap between its international recognition and its local presence?

Maciek: Allow me to expand a little on the first part of your question, because it also illustrates the historical context of the changes that have taken place in Wrocław and throughout Poland over the past twenty-five years.

I listen with great interest and satisfaction to the stories and opinions of festivalgoers who have been coming here for twenty-five, twenty or fifteen years and who, from their own perspective, can observe the progress our country has made.

The surroundings of Sala Gotycka alone have changed dramatically. Plac Dominikański, now surrounded by modern buildings, is almost unrecognisable. Transport infrastructure, the airport, motorways, hotels, restaurants, cafés, restored historical buildings illuminated at night, and finally the relative safety of the streets: all these things have changed.

Living here, we hardly notice any of it anymore. It takes visitors who return once a year, and who can observe these developments from a certain distance, to make us aware of how much has happened.

I enjoy looking at our guests’ social media posts, where, alongside the concerts, they document their explorations of the city. Photographs of historical buildings, galleries, parks and interesting architecture appear alongside their festival experiences.

Thanks to them, I sometimes begin to see Wrocław through different eyes myself and rediscover its beauty. I become a kind of festival tourist, exploring my own city again alongside them. I know that sounds a little strange, but that’s genuinely how it feels.

As for recognition locally, WIF has long had a permanent place in the cultural calendar of Wrocław and Poland. Television crews appear, we occasionally receive coverage in the mainstream press, and the festival also features on radio.

Considering the niche character of industrial music and the culture surrounding it, I think we’re actually quite well recognised.

Of course, we are not a mass event, and we never will be. Nor have we ever had any ambition to become one.

Karo: Industrial music once confronted listeners with the sounds and consequences of mechanisation. Today, technology has become almost inseparable from human experience, and algorithms increasingly shape culture itself. Do you think industrial music still has the capacity to disturb, challenge or anticipate the world around us? Where do you hear that potential today?

Maciek: In my view, industrial music has always tried to function as a kind of conscience of its time, or perhaps even as something that provokes pangs of conscience.

It brought to light problems, complexes, histories and theories that had been swept under the carpet. It was a form of shock therapy, a psychoanalyst’s couch on which the troubled representative of Homo sapiens would lie down, allowing all those suppressed fears, traumas and stories to emerge from the subconscious.

Simply becoming aware of their existence was supposed to be the first step towards healing.

That may sound somewhat idealistic, but it’s precisely how I understand this music and the culture behind it. There is something of the Promethean myth in it: an attempt to bring something authentic into the light, some hidden truth, often uncomfortable and difficult to accept.

Technology, or rather our dependence on it, is only one of many subjects, and not necessarily the most important one.

I see the contemporary potential of industrial music precisely in its ability to uncover what remains concealed.

It can operate on a deeply personal level, touching upon our feelings, emotions, fears, disorientation and growing isolation in an increasingly technologically dominated world.

But it can also reach much further, into the fields of social engineering, media manipulation, politics, omnipresent algorithms and artificial intelligence, which today is perceived simultaneously as an opportunity and a potential threat to our existence.

The world is accelerating towards a future in which almost everything is becoming increasingly difficult to predict. Much of that acceleration is driven by our own impulses, often ones we aren’t even conscious of.

That’s why I believe industrial music has even more to say today than it did fifty years ago, when Throbbing Gristle were recording their first album.

Karo: After so many editions, WIF has inevitably developed its own canon, traditions and audience expectations. How do you prevent that accumulated history from becoming a creative limitation? Is there a danger that a festival dedicated to experimentation can eventually become too comfortable with its own identity?

Maciek: I think the greatest danger facing any festival with an established history is falling into a routine and becoming convinced that something which worked in the past will necessarily work equally well every subsequent time.

It’s very easy to fall into the trap of reproducing your own success: inviting the same artists, staying within a familiar aesthetic and giving the audience exactly what it expects.

I’ve never regarded WIF as a museum of industrial music or a place devoted exclusively to preserving its purist form. Of course, we have our own canon, but WIF has always been characterised by a rather eclectic programme. In fact, eclecticism is practically our middle name.

On our stages, artists representing seemingly distant genres appear on equal terms: old-school industrial, noise, dark ambient, neofolk, power electronics, EBM, rhythm’n’industrial, post-punk and avant-garde music.

Experimentation doesn’t necessarily mean searching for something completely new, unknown or avant-garde at any cost. The return of an artist who hasn’t appeared at WIF for many years can be just as interesting as presenting a recently established project.

What matters to me is that there should be an idea and a genuine artistic motivation behind every choice, rather than simply a desire to tick another name off a list.

Nor do I feel particularly obliged to fulfil the audience’s expectations. Naturally, I have enormous respect for our audience, and I’m delighted that people have continued returning to Wrocław for so many years, but I wouldn’t want them to be the ones programming the festival.

There is, however, a moment after every edition when we open ourselves up to suggestions in WIF’s private Facebook group. And believe me, usually two or three bands from that collection of ideas eventually find their way into the following year’s programme.

My role, however, is primarily to offer audiences something that I personally consider interesting: sometimes risky, sometimes difficult to appreciate, and sometimes simply surprising.

A good example would be the appearance of the post-punk group WIRE in 2013, which some people described as “Maciek’s middle age crisis line-up.”

Well, not everything has to appeal to everyone.

Can a festival become a prisoner of its own identity? Of course it can.

But I believe the antidote is simple curiosity about the world, openness towards new phenomena and a willingness to question your own habits as well.

I wouldn’t want WIF to become a festival that feels obliged to prove every year that it’s fashionable or up to date. Equally, I have no intention of reproducing the same lineups every couple of years merely to satisfy the broadest and least demanding section of the audience.

Karo: Curating a festival also means making choices that won’t necessarily please everyone. Have you ever included an artist because you believed the audience needed to be challenged, rather than entertained? And has your own definition of what belongs at WIF changed over the years?

Maciek: In the beginning, I would simply stand in front of my record collection and wonder whom I would like to see performing in Wrocław. Then I’d write to them.

WIF was my own project, something that allowed me to fulfil my dreams of seeing musicians whose work I loved perform live and meeting them personally.

I wanted to create a festival that I would be willing to travel to myself, even to the other side of the world. A festival with a lineup unlike those of other events, eclectic but still orbiting around a common artistic centre.

A festival without a rigid division between headliners and support acts, and whose programme wasn’t dictated by fashionable music websites, booking agencies or record labels.

These days, I stand in front of that symbolic record collection rather less frequently. My ideas come primarily from my own knowledge and taste, but also from the need to maintain the right degree of diversity.

I wouldn’t want the festival to sound too monotonous. Eclecticism supported by quality is one of the fundamental principles I follow when assembling the programme, although I’ve already mentioned that.

Apart from being an organiser, I’m also a musician. I’ve performed at numerous festivals in Poland and across Europe, and there’s one thing I know very well: how I would like to be treated by other organisers.

I also remember occasions when I was unhappy with the way I was treated, and I try to learn from those experiences.

I want everyone at our festival, both onstage and behind the scenes, to feel the way I would want to feel when performing somewhere myself.

Naturally, that doesn’t mean allowing absolutely everything or letting one of the bands walk all over you.

I believe in the principle of reciprocal energy: what you give is what you receive. Energy has to circulate between both sides; there has to be an exchange. This applies equally to organisers and artists.

I’ve never been an industrial purist. Sometimes people have criticised me for inviting artists who supposedly don’t play industrial music.

But I’ve always considered industrial to be a doorway opening onto various forms of dark electronic music, and not exclusively electronic music.

As I’ve already mentioned, we also present post-punk and neofolk artists.

When selecting performers, their attitude and artistic roots matter more to me than any genre label. What projects were they previously involved in? What kind of artistic environment did they come from? Who inspires them?

These are the questions that interest me.

Karo: Industrial culture has a complicated history of provocation, political ambiguity and uncomfortable imagery. In today’s increasingly polarised cultural climate, how do you distinguish meaningful artistic confrontation from empty provocation? Has your understanding of curatorial responsibility changed?

Maciek: I’m not going to attempt to establish some universal boundary between artistic provocation and provocation for its own sake.

I’ve always believed that art should have room for ambiguity, irritation, uncomfortable questions and the crossing of boundaries.

In industrial culture, provocation has been one of the tools of artistic expression from the very beginning. It was never simply about shocking people, but primarily about provoking a response, confronting the audience with something they might otherwise prefer to ignore or repress.

As I mentioned earlier, I see industrial music as a form of shock therapy.

As a curator, however, I don’t want to act as a censor or an arbiter. I have no intention of filtering art exclusively through the question of whether it is comfortable, politically correct or consistent with current expectations.

What matters to me is the context, the artistic intention and whether there is something behind a particular statement beyond the desire to cause a scandal. Whether it is authentic.

But I don’t necessarily have to agree with an artist to recognise that their presence in the programme makes sense.

I wouldn’t want WIF to become a place where we present only things that are safe, comfortable and relatively easy to appreciate.

Karo: Twenty-five editions must contain countless stories that never made it into festival reports or photographs. Beyond the performances themselves, what do you think has shaped WIF most profoundly? Is there a decision, failure or seemingly insignificant encounter that changed its course without the audience ever realising it?

Maciek: Whenever I watch the video trailer accompanying this year’s anniversary edition of WIF, made in the style of the opening sequence from Star Wars, a particular thought comes to mind.

Instead of a story about something that happened a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away, the screen shows name after name disappearing into outer space: almost five hundred bands that performed at WIF between 2001 and 2026.

I see every one of those names as a separate story.

Each name carries its own memories. Behind each one are dozens of exchanged emails, stories from rehearsals, concerts and everything that happened away from the stage.

The overwhelming majority of those memories, probably around 93 percent, are pleasant and positive, although naturally there have also been less enjoyable experiences and some rather funny situations.

I think it is precisely all those encounters, relationships and events, rather than the concerts alone, that have shaped WIF most profoundly.

One day I’ll write a book about it, with the working title WIF Offstage. For now, I’m quietly taking notes and not revealing any details.

Karo: Looking ahead, what would you be willing to change, abandon or completely reinvent to keep WIF artistically relevant? And what would you still like to experience at the festival that hasn’t happened yet?

Maciek: Apart from rational analysis, which is often extremely helpful when organising an undertaking of this kind, I remain faithful to my intuition.

So far, it has never let me down. It tells me, as situations arise, what to give up, what to avoid getting involved in and where it’s worth taking a risk.

After all these years, there’s also one thing I know for certain: I have no ambition to create something that is the biggest, the most expensive, the most fashionable or the most avant-garde.

I don’t want to participate in that endless competition to be the most of everything.

I believe our festival is appropriately scaled, we have a wonderful location and an open-minded audience, and there’s still a long list of interesting artists waiting to be presented.

What more could I possibly want?

Perhaps only enough strength and good health to keep this whole thing going for a little while longer.

About Maciek Frett

Maciek (Maciej) Frett is a Polish musician, cultural curator and festival director based in Wrocław. Active since the mid-1990s, he is a co-founder of the audiovisual post-industrial project Job Karma, whose work combines electronic composition, field recordings and visual experimentation with an interest in the social, political and psychological consequences of modern civilisation.

He is also involved in 7JK, a collaboration with British musician Matt Howden of Sieben, and records under his own name as Frett, with solo releases including “The World As A Hologram” (2020) and “NOTTWO” (2023), exploring experimental electronics, rhythmic structures and sound production.

Beyond his musical activities, Frett co-founded Wrocław Industrial Festival in 2001 and is its artistic director. He has organised the festival every year since 2003, when it moved into Sala Gotycka in Wrocław, and has run further cultural initiatives through Industrial Art, including the festivals Podwodny Wrocław, Rytuał and Energia Dźwięku. The 2026 edition, held from 5 to 8 November, marked WIF’s 25th anniversary, bringing together SPK in its new SPKtR incarnation, collaborations between Flint Glass and Ah Cama-Sotz, and between Meta Meat and N.U. Unruh, and an international audience that has grown around the event over more than two decades.

Official festival website: industrialart.eu

items.title: Supreme Court – Full Of Unsaid Words (Digital/CD Album – Infacted Recordings)
items.summary: Kay Härtel remains the driving force behind Supreme Court. Having previously been involved with the...
items.fullText:
Kay Härtel remains the driving force behind Supreme Court. Having previously been involved with the more EBM-oriented project DavaNtage, he has now reached his fifth official album under the Supreme Court moniker.

The album consists of 13 tracks that immediately draw the listener into a Dark-Electro-infused world. However, this is far from a standard genre exercise, as atmosphere and melodic lines play a significant role in the compositions. Rather than relying on brute force, the album unfolds as an atmospheric experience that transports the listener into an imaginary nightmare. The compositions are well-crafted, consistently revealing a distinctively dark and melodic character. While the vocals generally lean towards the harsh, typically Dark-Electro style, I personally found myself gravitating towards the harder tracks. That said, there are also some fine, more subdued moments, such as “Behind Your Doors,” which even brings Project Pitchfork to mind.

Although the album lacks a truly defining climax, it is, in my view, yet another successful release. (Rating:7½).

Listen to “Freak On A Leash”:

About Supreme Court

Supreme Court is a dark electro project from Chemnitz, Germany, started in 1996 by Kay Härtel with Marcus Tischer. Härtel, who also runs the project DavaNtage, has kept Supreme Court on Infacted Recordings across its recent catalogue. The band issued “Yell It Out” in 2005 and “Hypocrites + Saints” in 2007, then moved to Infacted for “Keep Calm + Carry On” in 2009 and “Avid for Revenge” in 2022. On stage the line-up expands to include Enrico Kunze and Sebastian Nebel.

The act has appeared on the German electro circuit, including a slot on the 17th Elektrisch Festival bill in 2025. “Full of unsaid Words” is the fifth Supreme Court studio album, reaching listeners in 2026 as the project’s first full-length since “Avid for Revenge” in 2022.

items.title: Cold Hearted Festival 2026: Five Editions, Two Stages and the Art of Divided Attention
items.summary: Karo Kratochwil reviews Cold Hearted Festival's fifth edition in Dresden on 14 November 2026, with HUIR, Night In Athens and Paradox Obscur among eleven acts.
items.fullText:
Cold Hearted Festival returned to Dresden’s Alter Schlachthof on 14 November 2026 for its fifth edition. The programme brought together eleven projects from different generations and geographical backgrounds across two stages. Since its beginnings in 2022, Cold Hearted Festival has built four consecutive sell-outs and a prominent position on the European dark alternative calendar, this year’s programme demonstrating the breadth of a scene that continues to develop well beyond its original stylistic boundaries.

Such consistency is notable in an environment where independent festivals must negotiate rising production costs, demanding logistics and the challenge of maintaining a recognisable identity without letting their programmes become predictable. Cold Hearted combined established artists with newer projects whose musical backgrounds extend into alternative rock, industrial electronics, underground club culture and hip-hop.

Cold Hearted Festival 2026: eleven acts, two stages

The fifth edition also exposed one of the less fortunate consequences of the festival’s ambitions. With eleven performances distributed between two stages and most of them overlapping, the evening demanded a near-impossible series of decisions: stay with one artist, or leave a performance midway through to catch part of another. For those trying to see as much as possible, the festival became an exercise in constant movement between rooms, with little opportunity to absorb an entire concert before the next decision arrived.

This report reflects that fragmented experience, combining detailed impressions of the performances followed most closely with observations of the wider programme. The contrasts between artists were often pronounced enough to make even these interrupted encounters revealing.

HUIR, Darkways and the night’s early contrasts

The first difficult decision arrived at 17:00, when two Barcelona projects, HUIR and Darkways, opened the programme simultaneously. Both had been among the concerts drawing the most attention, for different reasons.

Having followed HUIR’s development, reviewed their recordings and previously interviewed Ana Of The Head and David Solazo, encountering their music live was especially welcome. Their early EP “Triumphal Arch Lovers” and subsequent debut album “States Of Light”, released through Cold Transmission Music in May 2026 with production by Maurizio Baggio, had already established a musical language in which post-punk’s introspective tendencies coexist with the more luminous possibilities of synthpop. What has consistently distinguished their compositions is an ability to accommodate sadness without letting it determine the entire emotional character of the music.

In Dresden, that quality showed through more than the arrangements: it also showed through the care given to the duo’s presentation. HUIR appeared in elaborate costumes, surrounded by atmospheric lighting that complemented the music’s considered aesthetic. The result was cinematic without producing a sense of artificial distance; the performance retained an appealing intimacy, suggesting the duo’s visual interest originates in the same creative sensibility that informs the songwriting.

Ana’s voice was central to that impression, with a natural warmth and expressive flexibility that let the music move from wistful introspection toward passages of greater rhythmic confidence without requiring dramatic changes in vocal technique. David’s guitar introduced a more elusive quality, its melodic lines sometimes carrying a lingering sadness, elsewhere supplying a gentle counterpoint to the synthesizers; the restraint of his playing meant the guitar rarely demanded attention through sheer prominence, yet its presence frequently changed a composition’s emotional colour.

HUIR were among the evening’s personal highlights. Their performance’s elegance was matched by genuine musical substance, and its expressive delicacy never diminished its underlying vitality.

Across the venue, Darkways pursued an altogether different approach, dispensing with elaborate visual presentation and placing the weight of their instrumental arrangements directly in the foreground. Darkways have been among the most rewarding musical discoveries of 2026, largely through their January album “Rust”, a record concerned with impermanence, mortality and the gradual erosion of identity. Their background in heavier guitar-oriented music gives their interpretation of darkwave a density and directness that separates it from projects primarily interested in electronic atmosphere.

The guitars in Dresden were outstanding, with a richness of tone and physical force that immediately commanded attention, their strength lying as much in melodic construction as in volume or distortion. Muscular passages gave way to more reflective phrases without disrupting the arrangements, and the synthesizers supplied additional depth without softening the music’s underlying character. Although the overlap with HUIR prevented experiencing either concert in full, Darkways are developing a musical identity of considerable substance, integrating heavier influences without surrendering darkwave’s melodic character.

The next part of the programme introduced Haunt Me, the San Antonio project founded in 2021 by vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Darius Davila, approaching gothic melancholy through a more traditional songwriting vocabulary. Now a trio, Haunt Me draw on post-punk, gothic rock and alternative music, with their 2025 album “Watch You Bleed” expanding the electronic dimensions of a sound still largely grounded in guitars and expressive vocal melodies. Their attachment to the architecture of the song itself shows in immediately discernible melodic lines and arrangements that support the vocal expression – a reminder of how familiar instrumental foundations can accommodate contemporary sensibilities.

The concurrent appearance of Skelesys presented an interesting contrast. Originally from Argentina and now based in Berlin, the musician and producer approaches post-punk from a background in electronic club culture, and his guitars become sources of tension, abrasion and rhythmic texture within largely electronic constructions. Recognisable post-punk elements are integrated into momentum that owes as much to the dancefloor as to the traditional rock arrangement, producing a sound that resists easy classification as either guitar music or club-oriented electronics.

A further departure from conventional darkwave arrived with GVLLOW, whose background in Southern California’s punk environment and subsequent involvement with underground hip-hop have produced one of the programme’s more unusual artistic trajectories. His incorporation of post-punk and gothic rock into that musical history depends precisely on the tensions between its influences, drawing on punk’s urgency, hip-hop’s rhythmic instincts and contemporary alternative production.

Meanwhile, the Chilean duo VIOFLESH, consisting of vocalist Vio and producer Flesh, approached electronic melancholy through a more intimate and sensual vocabulary. Their October 2026 album “Dark Bellow” explores desire, betrayal, fear and transformation, developing compositions in which electronic repetition provides a framework for emotionally charged vocal expression. The synthesizer patterns often possess an almost detached regularity, while Vio’s delivery introduces a far less predictable human element. The result is an impression of emotional instability beneath the apparently controlled arrangements. Their presence also broadened the festival’s geographical perspective: the contemporary coldwave vocabulary has been absorbed and reinterpreted far beyond its European origins.

Main stage: Ash Code, Night In Athens, Paradox Obscur and QUAL

By the time Ash Code appeared on the main stage, the programme had already travelled through a remarkable variety of interpretations of contemporary dark music. The Italian trio, formed in Naples in 2014, is a more established point of reference within the modern European darkwave revival, combining the urgency of programmed rhythms with post-punk’s characteristic instrumental restraint. Their 2025 album “Synthome”, written following a difficult period in the band’s history, brought questions of grief, survival and persistence into a familiar musical framework. Alongside She Past Away, Ash Code represent a generation of artists whose work helped establish much of the contemporary darkwave vocabulary subsequently explored by younger projects.

Ash Code’s appearance overlapped with Night In Athens, the project of Greek-born, London-based musician, composer and producer Tina Boleti, a scheduling conflict made less regrettable by a performance on the second stage that became one of the evening’s strongest memories. Side-Line interviewed Tina Boleti in 2024, and recordings such as “Metropolis”, “CRIME SEEN” and “Wasted Reflektions” reveal an artist fascinated by repetition, rhythmic severity and the psychological possibilities of vocal performance – qualities that became even more apparent live.

Performing alone imposes particular demands on an artist, especially when the music relies on programmed electronics and every gesture is immediately visible in the absence of other musicians. Boleti appeared entirely at ease within those conditions, commanding the stage with an intensity that never seemed dependent on exaggerated theatrical effects. The programmed rhythms could turn fierce and insistently physical, yet her singing retained an almost confessional quality, suggesting a personal narrative operating beneath the strict discipline of the electronic arrangements. The visual presentation, with rich colours and carefully preserved darkness, let her movements assume an almost sculptural quality. Moments of stillness became as expressive as the more vigorous passages. Night In Athens were among the absolute highlights of Cold Hearted.

The subsequent appearance of Paradox Obscur on the main stage offered another of the evening’s exceptional performances, with a substantially different musical character. The Athens-based duo of Kriistal Ann and Toxic Razor have spent more than a decade developing a sophisticated approach to synthesizer-based composition, drawing on minimal wave, synthpop, EBM and experimental electronics while retaining a pronounced interest in hardware instrumentation and real-time performance. Side-Line interviewed Paradox Obscur in February 2026, around the release of their sixth studio album, “IKONA”, issued through Metropolis Records in September 2025 and built on digital hardware synthesis, including wavetable and FM techniques, without abandoning the instrumental immediacy that distinguishes the duo’s work.

At Alter Schlachthof, those technical foundations produced a performance of notable clarity. Toxic Razor’s synthesizer arrangements had a formidable rhythmic presence that emerged less through excessive layering than through carefully controlled changes of timbre, melodic emphasis and internal movement. Kriistal Ann’s vocals, restrained and sometimes almost ethereal, prevented the more rigorous electronic arrangements from becoming emotionally remote. Deep, saturated red lighting surrounded the musicians and their instruments, transforming the stage into one of the festival’s most memorable visual environments.

The concurrent appearance of QUAL on the second stage introduced a markedly harsher interpretation of electronic music. As the solo project of William Maybelline, otherwise known for his work with Lebanon Hanover, QUAL inhabits an industrial territory in which the restrained minimalism and emotional distance associated with his better-known project give way to distortion, saturated bass frequencies and a more confrontational approach. Repetition becomes a source of pressure, heavily processed vocals acquire an unsettling quality, and the rhythmic structures are designed to be experienced as much physically as melodically.

The evening’s final performance belonged to She Past Away, whose position at the end of the programme provided a return to a musical language long associated with contemporary darkwave. Since the release of “Belirdi Gece” in 2012, the Turkish project has played a role in the international development of the genre, with hypnotic basslines, restrained guitar figures, programmed rhythms and Volkan Caner’s distinctive vocal delivery built around Turkish-language lyrics. She Past Away’s 2026 album “Mizantrop” continues the project’s exploration of introspection, isolation and alienation, extending a body of work whose influence can be traced across numerous contemporary artists.

A fifth edition that confirmed the festival’s identity

The fifth edition of Cold Hearted Festival ultimately confirmed the strength of an event whose programming reflects both an understanding of the scene and a willingness to accommodate its less conventional developments. The lineup was not uniform in aesthetic; its differences revealed how many musical possibilities now exist within the broader vocabulary of coldwave, post-punk and dark electronics.

The production deserves recognition too. Throughout the evening, the lighting contributed to the artistic character of the performances with unusual sensitivity, whether through the visual atmosphere surrounding HUIR, the carefully controlled darkness of Night In Athens or the saturated red illumination accompanying Paradox Obscur. These were not decorative additions, but instances where the visual environment changed how the music was experienced.

The extensive overlap between performances remains a real reservation. With a lineup of consistent quality, the need to move repeatedly between stages could become frustrating and physically exhausting, especially for visitors hoping to appreciate the musicians’ work with the attention it deserved. While the arrangement allows organisers to fit a larger programme into a limited period, it compromises the continuity of individual concerts, turning some of the evening’s most promising encounters into incomplete impressions.

The festival’s continuing popularity is nonetheless easy to understand. Its fourth consecutive sold-out Dresden edition reflects the loyalty of an audience prepared to support carefully considered independent programming, while its international character and stylistic variety have helped establish an identity extending beyond any particular group of headlining artists. Five editions in, Cold Hearted has become a meeting point for an international community whose musical interests continue to evolve – an anniversary programme that was ambitious, visually striking and rich in discoveries, even where the timetable made it difficult to give each act the attention it earned.

All photos: Karo Kratochwil.

items.title: Nico Amara releases album ‘Punishment Machinery’
items.summary: Swiss musician Nico Amara releases the post-industrial album "Punishment Machinery" digitally on 13 November 2026, inspired by Dante's Inferno.
items.fullText:
Swiss electronic musician Nico Amara released her second full-length album, “Punishment Machinery”, digitally on 13 November 2026, with CD and cassette editions to follow through Violet Hour Transmissions. The nine-track record traces a descent through selected circles of Dante’s Inferno, beginning in the dark wood and ending with an emergence from the depths.

The lyrics were written for specific passages of Dante’s “Inferno” before the music was completed, fixing the order of the nine pieces and requiring the music to develop around that structure. Its fragmented, multilingual and often violent texts confront destruction and punishment from a contemporary perspective, with the Inferno reflected as a vast machinery of punishment in both concept and sound. Musically, “Punishment Machinery” moves further toward minimalism: melodic material is heavily reduced, while mechanical rhythms and repetition are set against dense layers of noise, pushing Nico Amara’s darkwave foundations further into post-industrial territory.

Tracklist

  1. Inizio dalla fine
  2. Non-arrival
  3. Hate
  4. Non-believer
  5. Unbecome
  6. Burn
  7. Call in masks
  8. Fading
  9. At the end of it all

The album was preceded by two singles released from Dante’s own circles of Hell: “Burn”, drawn from the Seventh Circle and confronting environmental destruction and animal exploitation, released 25 September 2026 with an official video in October; and “Fading”, drawn from the Ninth Circle and the subject of betrayal, released 30 October 2026. Both tracks are also available individually on Bandcamp.

Credits

“Punishment Machinery” was written, performed and produced by Nico Amara. It was mixed and mastered by S. Templeton at Influx Studio, with cover art by Nico Amara and photography by J.A. Greant.

About Nico Amara

Nico Amara is a Bern, Switzerland-based solo darkwave and post-industrial project of composer and multidisciplinary artist Nicole Fior. The project released its debut full-length, “Constraints”, in August 2025. “Punishment Machinery” is Nico Amara’s second full-length, released digitally on 13 November 2026 and preceded by the singles “Burn” and “Fading”, with CD and cassette editions to follow through Violet Hour Transmissions. Built around a concept drawn directly from Dante’s “Inferno”, the album extends Nico Amara’s post-industrial direction with its most minimal and reduced songwriting to date.

items.title: TéMèT releases synthpop single ‘Not the Same Soul’
items.summary: TéMèT releases the synthpop single "Not the Same Soul" on 13 November 2026, the sixth release in the duo's Obsidian series.
items.fullText:
TéMèT, the Strasbourg synthpop and darkwave duo, released the single “Not the Same Soul” on all platforms on 13 November 2026. The track is catalogued as Obsidian VI in the duo’s ongoing singles series and closes a run that began with “Discord” (Obsidian IV, 21 August 2026) and continued with “What We Are” (Obsidian V, 2 October 2026).

“Not the Same Soul” is about time slipping by, growing up and losing the light, until the mirror shows someone no longer recognisable. Layered synths and an understated vocal are cut through by a guitar hook. The music was composed, performed and recorded by the duo in their own studio; the video’s visuals were created with AI tools.

All three tracks in the “Discord” / “What We Are” / “Not the Same Soul” run are collected together on Spotify.

TéMèT’s Obsidian singles series

TéMèT previously released “Discord” in August and “What We Are” in October, both covered on Side-Line: TéMèT – ‘Discord’ single and TéMèT – ‘What We Are’ single. The duo describes “Discord” as sitting between Depeche Mode and OMD.

About TéMèT

TéMèT is a synthpop and darkwave duo formed in Strasbourg, France, in 2022, made up of the two musicians K1 and MYK. The project’s name draws on Tem, the ancient Egyptian deity associated with the setting sun and with creation and endings. Its sound mixes a melodic, atmospheric register influenced by Depeche Mode with darker, more energetic material.

The duo debuted in 2022 with the single “Bad Night”, followed by “U Come I Come” and “All Inclusive (Radio Edit)”. From August 2026, TéMèT began numbering its singles as an ongoing “Obsidian” series: “Discord” (Obsidian IV, 21 August 2026), “What We Are” (Obsidian V, 2 October 2026) and “Not the Same Soul” (Obsidian VI, 13 November 2026). TéMèT composes, performs and records entirely in its own studio, and the visuals for its official videos are created with AI tools. With “Not the Same Soul” now out, the Obsidian series continues to build toward a fuller body of work from the duo.

items.title: From Bérèche You to Spectre Rebel: debut single ‘Wouldn’t You Like To Know’ out now
items.summary: Spectre Rebel, the new duo of Isak Rypdal and Thomas Caz, released debut single "Wouldn't You Like To Know" on 6 November 2026. Interview inside.
items.fullText:
(By our Norwegian correspondent. Photos by Thomas CA Brevik)

The band formerly known as Bérèche You is no more, as the guys behind it have done the phoenix manoeuvre and risen again as something familiar, only better! The Norwegian electro synthpop act Spectre Rebel debuts their rebirth with the single “Wouldn’t You Like To Know“, and I’m not the only one getting goosebumps from the Pet Shop Boys vibe and a little touch of acid in between the beats. The single was released on November 6th 2026 on Crab Key Records.

Spectre Rebel interview

Isak Rypdal and Thomas Caz tells us about the changes, the new track and more.

Side-Line: What does this name change from Bérèche You to Spectre Rebel signify? A step back to the Electro Spectre spirit, evolving into something new, or a bit of both?

Isak Rypdal: Bérèche You was initially based on instrumental works left over from Electro Spectre sessions and never used. The idea behind Bérèche You was to use the best tracks never used from Model1 or the Electro Spectre album sessions, inviting different singers to add their spirit to the tracks.

Spectre Rebel is a very different story, and is the cooperation between me and my good friend Thomas Caz, who’s also a great singer. The collaboration emerged from Thomas featuring on several songs from the Bérèche You sessions, and turned into the massive collaboration that involves three singles and two upcoming albums.

S-L: “Wouldn’t You Like To Know”, with its spoken word/rap vocals and production, differs a bit from previous projects – what made you go in this direction?

Thomas Caz: Every song is a new opportunity to explore melodies and lyrics. After letting ideas mull about for some time, inspiration usually leads to something worth exploring. In the case of WYLTK, the really nice bass rhythm more or less invited a more spoken word approach. The title is like a conclusion to the verses and provides a cheeky punch, coupled with a chorus that underscores the theme of the song.

The theme itself speaks of frustration in the face of hard times. How do you really cope? How do you get through? I bet you’d like to know the answer? So do I, and everyone else. Because we all just want to live and must remind ourselves to be optimistic. This is reflected in the up-tempo beat and energetic vibe.

S-L: I also read about the upcoming album, what do we have in store there?

IR: The new album “Midnight Sins” has been in development for the last 24 months and consists of 10 brand new songs that span from hard-hitting synthpop songs to deeper and more personal melodies.

TC: While some songs have a personal flair, they are sure to evoke resonance with many. We have aimed for a balance between hefty bangers and more downbeat vibes to create a complete album experience.

For “Midnight Sins” we have selected 10 of the best songs from the past 24 months. We have worked hard and honed each song to a high level of quality. We hope it will rank as a top album in the genre. This is one for all fans of modern synthpop!

The second upcoming album follows sometime later and is called “Alternate Universe”. It will present some super remixes, plus several new songs that we couldn’t fit on “Midnight Sins”. The two albums are really one in two parts.

S-L: What’s next from Spectre Rebel besides the album?

IR: Spectre Rebel will release the following single “Shelter In The Rain” on November 27th, featuring a brand new music video which premieres the same day.

Out now on these platforms: Spotify | Apple Music | TIDAL | Deezer | YouTube | QQ Music

About Spectre Rebel

Spectre Rebel is the Norwegian synthpop duo of producer Isak Rypdal and singer and songwriter Thomas Caz, the artist name of Thomas C. A. Brevik. The music continues Rypdal’s “Spectre” line of projects and, in songwriting and production, follows on from the “Stereo Dreams” album series by Electro Spectre. Brevik writes the duo’s melodies and lyrics, and has created artwork, visuals and live photography for several of Rypdal’s projects over the years.

Rypdal has been active since the early 1990s. In 1999 he signed his project Doctor No to Warner Music Norway. The singles “Lastima” and “La Luna” (2000), co-written with bandmate Bendik Gjevjon, reached the Norwegian sales chart and received heavy rotation on Norwegian radio, including NRK P3. The album “Fat Sound To The Masses” followed in 2001, along with a deal with Warner Music Japan. The same year, Rypdal remixed Secret Garden’s Eurovision winner “Nocturne” for Universal Music’s “Grand Prix Party” compilation. In 2003 he teamed up with singer Hanne Romsaas as Freeloader. Their single “Pure Devotion”, published via EMI Publishing Germany, made Judge Jules’ top ten on BBC Radio 1, and was followed by “Two Become One” (2004) and “Come Dance With Me” (2006). Rypdal’s live work includes the “We Love The 90’s” concerts and more than 100 shows around the world.

In 2009 Rypdal formed Electro Spectre in Oslo with singer and lyricist Alexander Bjørneboe. The duo released the albums “Watch It All Turn” (2009), “Dangerous Game” (2012), “Bullets & Desert Blooms” (2014), “Beautiful Lies” (January 2016) and “A Man-Made Sun” (October 2018). Electro Spectre made its live debut at the ElectroStat festival at Maanefisken in Oslo in October 2010, playing before headliner Mesh, and has since supported OMD, Marsheaux, Zeromancer, Covenant and Melotron, among others. In November 2018 the band signed a 15-year contract with Meisel Musikverlage in Berlin. “Stereo Dreams Pt1“, the first part of the “Stereo Dreams” trilogy, followed on 16 September 2022 on Crab Key Records, Rypdal’s own label, in collaboration with Meisel Music. Alongside Electro Spectre, Rypdal launched Model1, with the album “The Vocoders Strikes Back” (August 2016) and a Depeche Mode tribute album (2017), and Kist, a collaboration with singer Christine Litle that released “Musickist” in 2016.

In spring 2024 Rypdal started Bérèche You, a project that invited different singers onto unused tracks from the Model1 and Electro Spectre sessions. Brevik made his vocal debut there under the name Cassiel Agrippa on the single “Someone Like Me“, and the album “Business Of Love“, which also features Madil Hardis, followed on 10 May 2024. The second album, “The Price Of Love“, came out on 14 February 2025 with Cassiel Agrippa as the only vocalist. On 21 February 2025 Rypdal and Brevik played their first live show together, as Bérèche You, supporting Henric de la Cour at Goldie in Oslo.

Spectre Rebel’s debut single “Wouldn’t You Like To Know” was released on Crab Key Records on 6 November 2026, ahead of the album “Midnight Sins” in January 2027.

items.title: “See the Smiles Crack Behind the Masks” — Bristol’s Twin Cynic Examines the People We Pretend to Be on “Identity Crisis”
items.summary: Ghostly actors losing shape and form See the smiles crack Behind the masks Nothing but harlequins playing aristocrats Everybody’s performing for somebody, even when the audience has gone home. We… The post “See the Smiles Crack Behind the Masks” — Bristol’s Tw
items.fullText:
Ghostly actors losing shape and form

See the smiles crack

Behind the masks

Nothing but harlequins playing aristocrats

Everybody’s performing for somebody, even when the audience has gone home. We rehearse conversations in the bathroom mirror, manufacture personalities for people we barely tolerate, and spend an astonishing percentage of our lives pretending to possess convictions we abandoned sometime around breakfast. The great modern preoccupation with authenticity has turned being yourself into another full-time occupation, complete with costumes, carefully prepared statements, and the nagging suspicion that somebody else has been handed a better script. Even our private misery seems to require an appropriate public presentation. One wonders whether Shakespeare, confronted with the current state of human affairs, might have simply shut down the Globe to get pissed somewhere.

On Identity Crisis, the debut album from Twin Cynic, the solo project of musician TJ Higgs, this exhausting theatre of existence becomes the setting for eleven examinations of identity, alienation, desire, mortality, and the desperate need to belong somewhere. Higgs, whose musical background includes years performing in metal bands, has turned his attention toward synth-driven post-punk, darkwave, and alternative rock. The resulting album suggests Depeche Mode meeting Japan somewhere in the vicinity of Interpol, with considerable guitar muscle and a taste for philosophical trouble. His previous experience with heavier music remains apparent in the force of his riffs, although the emotional concerns here require a more varied vocabulary.

The buoyant synth rhythm opening Star Fairy seems to carry some of adolescence’s careless confidence, with an alternative-rock riff falling into step and little guitar flourishes skipping ahead of the beat. Cooler electronics gather underneath as Higgs begins to sing with a sweetness that makes the recollections of cigarettes, Bowie songs, amusement parks, and afternoons beside the sea feel close enough to touch. The affection in his delivery gives each detail its own small importance; these are the things two people did together before either understood how finite their time might be. As the lyrics turn toward his friend’s death and the questions left unanswered, that easy forward motion becomes especially affecting. The rhythm still has somewhere to go, carrying memories of somebody who no longer does. Imagining his friend dancing among the stars, Higgs allows the song’s warmth to accommodate the loss without pretending to resolve it.

Warbling electronics, a bubbling beat, and deep, rhythmic bass introduce Cinema, while dream-pop guitar flourishes lend the opening a polished romantic sheen. Higgs sounds more assertive here, giving the lovers’ rehearsed exchanges an edge of accusation. Beneath all that attractive presentation, intimacy has become another opportunity to manipulate the casting. The guitars gain weight around the chorus, pressing against the tidy electronic arrangement as the lyrics move through forced smiles, scripted romance, and the humiliations of playing a part somebody else has written. A vocal sigh and a guitar solo briefly interrupt the proceedings before verse and chorus return, pulling the couple back into their familiar scenes. Even the song’s structure seems to appreciate how readily people repeat a disastrous performance when they remain convinced that the next take will be better. Everybody wants the lead; accepting responsibility for the script proves considerably less popular.

The first chimes and uneasy synth exhalations of Sin By Silence suggest trouble behind a carefully maintained facade. A low, sensual grunt precedes the entrance of a dark synth-pop beat, its mechanical precision recalling the early electronic arrangements of Depeche Mode’s A Broken Frame. Clipped keyboard figures and giallo-like synthesizer patterns keep a sense of threat circulating beneath the tune. Higgs moves between a heated croon and a more measured, Mode-like delivery, giving the song an outward composure suited to its examination of concealed abuse. False smiles and polite gestures become practical tools for avoiding an inconvenient truth; everyone can carry on looking respectable provided nobody asks what that respectability costs. The arrangement’s controlled movements make the implication particularly ugly. Cruelty can flourish in a room full of apparently reasonable people, especially when they have agreed that acknowledging it would spoil the atmosphere.

A deep spoken introduction opens Stardust, followed by low-lit synthesizer tones, shuffling percussion, bell-like accents, and a bassline with enough physical presence to keep the contemplation of extinction firmly attached to the body. Staccato electronics bring another suggestion of giallo unease, while Higgs lends his singing an ornate, almost baroque romance. Around him, Cocteau Twins-like guitar flourishes give the song a sense of distance and suspension, interrupted by heavier passages that alternate sustained notes with tightly chugging builds. Those changes in weight suit lyrics considering the eventual dissolution of bodies, galaxies, and everything between them: matter briefly gathers, acquires a name, and eventually disperses. His affectionate resignation makes that prospect strangely companionable. There is room for tenderness even in the thought of returning to elementary particles, although the guitars retain an appropriately forceful attachment to being alive. Oblivion can wait until the arrangement has finished making its case.

Breaking glass and overlapping human voices usher in People Are People, with the familiar drum pattern soon organizing the commotion. Higgs gives the Depeche Mode song a heavier centre of gravity, putting guitars in charge of the main melody while brass-like synthesizers remain audible beneath their weight. The combination lends the cover an artful gothic-rock character, and his delivery follows its own course: the verses sit closer to Dave Gahan’s phrasing, while the chorus takes on a more angular, art-rock cadence. These choices give the plea for basic human tolerance a bruised, exhausted quality. More than forty years after the original, the question at its centre still requires an answer, and Higgs sounds painfully aware of how many opportunities the species has had to provide one. Each return of the chorus carries the frustration of explaining the obvious to people who have made a career of avoiding it.

Rippling synthesizers and a sharp guitar attack open the doors to At The Masquerade, where Higgs croons over a steady electronic beat and thick bass. Each returning guitar figure seems to send another elaborate disguise tumbling across the ballroom. Skeletons promenade, smiles fracture, and the guests’ aristocratic airs begin to look like expensive methods of managing panic. Shakespeare’s theatre of human behaviour supplies an apt reference for this gathering, with everybody performing status while quietly dreading exposure. A break leaves the voice surrounded by bright, bubbling electronics, briefly lifting the guitars away from the spectacle before the chorus brings their attack back. That moment of relative exposure suits a song so preoccupied with what happens when the presentation fails. Beneath the decorations and social climbing sits a thoroughly democratic appointment with death, which has presumably neglected to observe the dress code.

A deeper, rippling synth melody, phased electronics, and dream-pop guitars give Cherry And Almond an inviting first taste. Higgs settles into a seductive croon above a low, funky bass shuffle, making temptation sound like an entirely reasonable way to spend the evening. As harmonies lift the chorus, the guitars grow heavier, bringing physical force to an attraction whose consequences are already becoming difficult to ignore. The lyrics’ sweetness and intoxication find a persuasive musical accomplice in that polished surface, with betrayal waiting beneath it. Around two-thirds of the way through, his delivery gathers into a fast, rhyming passage with a beat-poetry cadence, as though desire has talked itself past every available objection. An expressive guitar solo follows, giving the accumulated appetite another outlet. Knowing that an encounter is likely to end badly has rarely stopped anybody from ordering a second drink, and this song has already found the bottle.

With Terpsichore, a strummed post-punk guitar figure gives way to a stronger, immediately memorable riff, its momentum reinforced by cold synthesizers and busy, hissing drums. Named for the Greek muse of dance, the song follows an apprehensive arrival at a nightclub, where the crowd initially resembles a gathering of vampires and joining in requires a small act of nerve. Higgs sings with a heated intimacy as the guitar occasionally withdraws into little echoes of its central phrase, leaving room for his voice before the full riff rejoins the crooning chorus. The arrangement makes the surrender to movement feel cumulative: each return loosens another inhibition. Later, looping guitar tones and mounting drum tension intensify the sensation of a body outrunning its owner’s embarrassment. By the time ordinary consciousness threatens to reassert itself, dancing has supplied a convincing argument for spending a little less time supervising every gesture.

A steady rhythm section and an insistent guitar melody set Howling At The Moon in motion, with cold synthesizers underneath. When Higgs begins to sing, the guitar shifts into a clipped, ska-like offbeat before the arrangement changes direction again, letting bubbling electronic colours move beneath his croon. The successive shifts suit lovers whose freedom depends on circumstances changing around them. Selene’s moon grants a temporary interval of acceptance, while Apollo’s daylight promises the return of the judgments keeping them apart. Higgs gives their stolen hours a sense of movement and pleasure, including exuberant vocal whoops that release some of the tension accumulated in the verses. A catchy guitar solo later extends that exhilaration. Throughout, the persistent rhythm lends urgency to the pleasure: the night is passing, and every minute enjoyed together belongs to a freedom the morning will attempt to revoke.

The low, dream-pop guitar treatment introducing North Star provides a soft foundation for a heavier melody that climbs and falls above it. As Higgs begins to croon, that more forceful guitar recedes, leaving the treated chords and cold, bell-like synthesizer figures to support a song about finding direction through the memory of somebody absent. The arrangement gives that presence a convincing shape: guidance can be felt even when its source remains beyond reach. His voice rises with the chorus, extending the reassurance into an invitation to venture beyond familiar ground. Bowie returns to the album’s celestial vocabulary, linking music, affection, and the private ways people continue conversations that physical separation has interrupted. The earlier guitar weight gives those gentler passages a useful sense of support. Continuing requires courage, and Higgs allows the remembered voice of a loved one to supply a little of it.

Bell-like synth figures recalling A Broken Frame meet the sleek keyboard atmosphere of Duran Duran’s The Chauffeur on Beautiful Nonsense. Soft electronic sighs move underneath Higgs’s relaxed synth-pop phrasing, while the heavier guitars settle into a gentle background rumble. The arrangement has space to breathe, making an apt setting for lyrics about language finding its way onto the page, ideas taking shape through experiment, and inspiration returning after creative exhaustion. After so many examinations of performance and disguise, the pleasure of making something offers Higgs a place where uncertainty can be put to use. A romantic guitar solo rises late in the song, giving the closing stretch an expressive release without crowding its reflective pace. The album leaves him with words still to arrange and possibilities still to pursue, a modestly hopeful state of affairs for somebody who has spent eleven songs considering the difficulties of being a person.

Listen to Identity Crisis below and order the album here.

Across these eleven tracks, Twin Cynic’s Identity Crisis develops a consistent fascination with the gap between personal experience and public presentation. Higgs moves from individual grief to collective responsibility, from the absurdity of romantic performance to the magnificent indifference of the cosmos, examining how people construct identities to survive their relationships with others. The combination of synthesizers, forceful guitars, and emotionally direct songwriting gives these concerns an accessible musical framework, informed by the dramatic sensibilities of classic darkwave and post-punk.

The album has a persuasive willingness to admit that the search for identity can be a thoroughly ridiculous enterprise. We want to be recognized, adored, understood, and occasionally left completely alone, preferably without having to explain the contradictions. We invent versions of ourselves for lovers, strangers, employers, and friends, then wonder why the resulting collection of personalities feels increasingly difficult to reconcile.

Identity Crisis ultimately finds its consolation in the relationships, memories, and creative impulses that survive our attempts to define ourselves. The costumes may change, the audience may disappear, and the performers will eventually leave the stage. In the meantime, somebody has to write the songs, somebody has to dance, and somebody ought to have the decency to tell us when our masks have started slipping.

Catch Twin Cynic on 28 November at The Old England in Bristol, supporting PitFeeders.
